summary: High priest Ananias arrives in Caesarea with elders and the advocate Tertullus, who flatters Felix and charges Paul with sedition, leadership of the Nazarenes, and attempted temple profanation. Paul answers that only twelve days have passed, no crowd or disturbance can be proved, and his accusers from Asia are absent. He openly confesses worshiping Israel's ancestral God according to the Way, believing Torah and Prophets, and sharing the resurrection hope of just and unjust. Felix, already informed about the Way, postpones judgment. With his Jewish wife Drusilla he later hears Paul reason about faith in Christ, justice, self-control, and coming judgment. Frightened yet unmoved, Felix hopes for a bribe, repeatedly summons Paul, and leaves him imprisoned for two years to gain favor.
whyItMatters: Paul's defense refuses the premise that following the Way means abandoning Israel's God or Scriptures. The chapter also exposes how legal language can mask political convenience: Felix knows enough to delay, hears an ethically dangerous message, seeks money, and trades a prisoner's freedom for favor. Roman procedure sometimes restrains violence, but it does not guarantee justice.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator presenting the first Caesarean hearing and prolonged delay
context.audience: Readers evaluating forensic rhetoric, claims about the Way, resurrection hope, and compromised Roman governance
context.date: During Felix's governorship, before Festus succeeds him around AD 59–60
context.setting: The governor's court and custody arrangements in Caesarea
context.literaryForm: Formal prosecution and defense speeches followed by private hearing and delay summary

outline.heading: Tertullus flatters Felix and accuses Paul of sedition and profanation
Paul denies the facts while confessing the Way and resurrection hope
Felix delays, fears Paul's ethical message, seeks a bribe, and leaves him bound

keyVerses.text: But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets;
keyVerses.why: Paul explicitly presents the Way as worship of Israel's ancestral God in scriptural continuity.

keyVerses.text: In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.
keyVerses.why: Resurrection hope produces an accountable present discipline, not speculation alone.

keyVerses.text: As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, “Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.”
keyVerses.why: The judge becomes the morally examined person, yet fear never matures into justice.

questions.question: What is Tertullus doing in his opening?
questions.answer: As a rhētōr—advocate or orator—he begins with conventional captatio benevolentiae, winning the judge's goodwill through elaborate praise. His claims that Felix created great peace and reforms are especially flattering given ancient reports of Felix's brutality and unrest. Paul answers with a briefer acknowledgment of Felix's experience rather than matching the exaggeration.

questions.question: What charges are brought against Paul?
questions.answer: Tertullus frames him as a worldwide pest, a mover of sedition among Jews, a ringleader of the Nazarenes, and someone who attempted to profane the temple. The categories escalate a theological dispute into imperial public-order and sacred-space offenses. Paul's defense targets evidence: time was short, he disputed with no one, raised no crowd, and the original Asian accusers are absent.

questions.question: What does ‘sect of the Nazarenes’ mean?
questions.answer: Hairesis means a party, school, faction, or sect before the English word ‘heresy’ acquires its later technical sense. ‘Nazarenes’ identifies Jesus-followers through Jesus of Nazareth. Paul accepts that opponents call the Way a hairesis but rejects the implication that it is apostasy from Israel's God and Scriptures.

questions.question: Why is Acts 24:6–8 longer in this edition than in many modern Bibles?
questions.answer: Later textual witnesses add or preserve wording that the Jews wanted to judge Paul by their law, but Lysias violently intervened and ordered accusers to come; the WEB includes much of this expansion across verses 6–8, with verse 7 blank in its numbering. Earlier major Greek witnesses have the shorter transition. The longer reading sharpens blame of Lysias but does not change the hearing's main charges.

questions.question: How does Paul define the Way in relation to Judaism?
questions.answer: He says he worships ‘the God of our fathers,’ believes everything according to Torah and Prophets, came with alms and offerings, underwent purification, and shares his accusers' hope in resurrection of just and unjust. His disputed claim is the fulfillment of that hope in Jesus, not adoption of a foreign god.

questions.question: What does ‘resurrection of both just and unjust’ add?
questions.answer: The phrase widens resurrection beyond vindication of believers to universal accountability. It explains why Paul immediately says he trains his conscience to avoid offense toward God and people. Future judgment motivates present ethical practice rather than date calculation.

questions.question: Who are Felix and Drusilla?
questions.answer: Antonius Felix was a former imperial freedman governing Judea, remembered by ancient sources for corrupt and violent rule. Drusilla was a Jewish Herodian princess, daughter of Agrippa I, who became Felix's wife after leaving another marriage. Paul's topics—justice, self-control, judgment—are therefore not abstract virtues but pointed speech before powerful listeners.

questions.question: Why does Felix keep summoning Paul if he is afraid?
questions.answer: He knows more accurately about the Way and hears Paul repeatedly, but also hopes Paul will offer chrēmata—money, a bribe. Curiosity, fear, greed, and political delay coexist. The chapter distinguishes emotional reaction from repentance: Felix dismisses the inconvenient moral claim and preserves leverage over the prisoner.

questions.question: Why is Paul left bound for two years?
questions.answer: Felix delays under the pretext of awaiting Lysias, grants Paul limited access, repeatedly hopes for money, and finally seeks favor with Judean leaders by leaving him imprisoned when Festus succeeds him. Acts makes the injustice explicit. Legal custody advances Paul toward Roman witness, but providential outcome does not turn corrupt detention into righteousness.

glossary.def: Party, school, faction, or sect; not yet limited to the later technical sense ‘heresy.’
A public label for Jesus-followers derived from Jesus of Nazareth.
